prize_parts.citation: for empirical evidence on how import competition reshapes local labour markets and the distribution of earnings and employment

statement.case_for: In my opening I put B002 first and B044 second. After the maturity arguments from colleagues, I now think B044 is the better prize case on common criteria. The China-shock papers (roughly 2013-2016) turned a first-order question, who bears the cost of trade integration and how labour markets adjust, into a credibly identified empirical result. The design uses local labour markets, exposure measures and long-horizon outcomes. It has been replicated and extended across countries, and it changed both the trade and labour fields and the policy debate. More than a decade of scrutiny has refined the magnitudes without overturning the central finding that adjustment is slow and costly. Attribution is also unusually clean: Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the joint authors of the core papers, so a three-person part fits the cap without leaving out a co-originator. I would anchor the citation on the trade-shock evidence, where credit is clean, and not on the broader task-based theory, whose lineage runs through people outside the credited set.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the contribution is empirical application and design rather than a new conceptual framework. The identification rests on shift-share-style instruments, which have known inference problems. The size and persistence of the effects are still debated, and some of the debate concerns how much is trade and how much is automation. Because the credited set also includes Katz, and the task-based strand sits partly with Acemoglu, who is already a laureate, the committee may see this as two partial prizes rather than one. B040 has a cleaner, older and more purely conceptual claim, and a committee that weights theory-driven mechanisms should take it seriously.

responses.point: Ranks B040 first as a foundational mechanism, with credit concentrated in Kiyotaki and Moore. He treats the financial-accelerator strand as already recognised, and he sees the task-based and trade-shock strands of B044 as separable, proposing Autor and Hanson with Dorn and Katz as plausible alternatives.
responses.response: I agree that the Kiyotaki-Moore attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, and that nearly thirty years of use means maturity is no obstacle. I place it just behind B044 for two reasons. First, the empirical test of collateral-constraint amplification is more indirect, and how much amplification the mechanism contributes quantitatively in macro models is still contested. Second, the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises narrows its marginal novelty. I accept his point that the trade-shock and task strands are separable. That is why I would write the citation around the trade-shock evidence, where Dorn's role is as central as Hanson's. Leaving Dorn out would be hard to defend scientifically.

responses.point: Ranks B044 first and proposes Autor, Katz and Hanson to cover both the task and skill-bias line and the trade-shock line. She also calls B002 the least mature of the top candidates.
responses.response: I agree on B002's maturity. It is the main reason I have moved it from first place to an alternative. I do not agree that Katz should replace Dorn. Katz's contribution is the earlier skill-bias and inequality literature, a different strand with a different attribution story. Taking that strand in would blend two achievements into one part and would drop a co-author of the core China-shock papers. If the committee wants the task and skill-bias strand recognised, it would need its own part, and the three-person cap makes that impractical with this configuration.

responses.point: Ranks B044 first and proposes Autor and Hanson as the most defensible pair. He ranks B002 second, with Chetty and Hendren as the clear core, and flags the identification limits of the instrument-based designs.
responses.response: I share his concern about shift-share inference, and I treat it as the main scientific reservation. The core finding has survived the follow-up debate on persistence and magnitude, and I think that is the relevant test. I would still include Dorn. He co-authored the central papers, and a two-name award would understate a three-way joint contribution. On B002, I agree that Chetty and Hendren are the right two-person core if the committee goes that way. I would not make it the first choice this year, mainly because of recency.

responses.point: Ranks B017 first as the founding of modern political economics, with Persson, Tabellini and Besley as the core. He acknowledges the proximity to the 2024 institutions prize and that Persson may have ties that need disclosure.
responses.response: I accept the scientific case for B017 as a coherent programme. I ranked it last on the shortlist because the cross-country identification of constitutional and electoral-rule effects is weaker than in B044, and the overlap with 2024 is not trivial. His point about the founding of a field is a fair one, and I would not rule the programme out in a later round. On Persson, I cannot verify ties from my own profile. I mention below that my own institution is IIES, and I leave B017 out of my configuration partly for that reason.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the trade-shock evidence and the task-based framework as one prize-sized achievement or two, and so whether Katz should be considered.
How persistent and how large the China-shock effects are under alternative specifications, and how much of the labour-market adjustment is trade rather than automation.
How much the 2024 prize on technology and institutions reduces the marginal case for a technology-and-inequality award.
Whether B002 should be preferred despite its recency, if the committee judges measurement with population-scale administrative data to be a lasting advance.
Whether B040 should be preferred for its cleaner two-person attribution and greater age, and how much the 2022 prize should count against it.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent for the preferred part. The supplied profile shows no co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Dorn or Hanson. I disclose that my research on capital-skill complementarity and technological change is intellectually adjacent to the skill-bias literature behind this ballot. I also co-author with committee members Timo Boppart and John Hassler, neither of whom is a candidate. I am at IIES in Stockholm, and I cannot verify from my profile whether any credited name on B017 has a connection to it. That ballot is not in my configuration or alternatives.
